questions.question: When can the factorisation be written as $A=LU$ instead of $PA=LU$?
options: Whenever $A$ is square and invertible.
Only when $A$ is already upper triangular.
When no row interchanges are needed.
When the first pivot $a_{11}$ is nonzero.

questions.question: If $L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\3&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $U=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&4\end{pmatrix}$, what is $LU$?
options: $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}5&1\\0&5\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}2&4\\6&4\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\6&7\end{pmatrix}$

questions.question: Which pair of methods is naturally used after LU decomposition to solve a system?
options: Back substitution followed by forward substitution.
Gauss-Jordan elimination on $A$ followed by Cramer's rule.
Forward substitution followed by back substitution.
Cofactor expansion followed by Sarrus' rule.

questions.question: Why does LU decomposition help when solving several systems with the same matrix $A$ but different right-hand sides?
options: The factorisation is reused; only triangular solves remain
It guarantees every right-hand side has the same solution.
The right-hand side becomes irrelevant.
The matrix $A$ no longer has to be multiplied by vectors.

questions.question: Solve using $L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $U=\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$ with $LUx=\begin{pmatrix}5\\14\end{pmatrix}$. What is $x$?
options: $\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}5\\4\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}-1\\2\end{pmatrix}$

questions.question: A student writes $A=LU$ even though a row swap was used during elimination. What is missing?
options: Nothing; a swap is absorbed into $L$, which stays lower triangular
A permutation matrix is needed on the right, as in $AP=LU$
A diagonal matrix $D$ is needed, as in $A=LDU$
A permutation matrix $P$ is needed, as in $PA=LU$

questions.question: Why is LU decomposition more than simply writing any matrix as a product of two matrices?
options: Both factors are always invertible, unlike in a general product.
The factors commute, so $LU=UL$, unlike a general product.
The factors are triangular and come from elimination.
Both factors are diagonal, so $A$ splits into its pivots.

questions.question: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$, why would pivoting be needed before a standard first elimination step?
options: $A$ is singular, so elimination must stop
The entry $0$ must first be scaled to $1$
A zero in column $1$ forces a column swap
The top-left pivot is $0$, so swap rows

questions.question: Gaussian elimination on a $2\times2$ matrix $\boldsymbol{A}$ needs no row swaps and uses one step: add $3$ times row $1$ to row $2$. What is $\boldsymbol{L}$ in $\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{L}\boldsymbol{U}$?
options: $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-3&1\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\3&1\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}1&-3\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\-3&0\end{pmatrix}$

questions.question: Suppose $\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{L}\boldsymbol{U}$ with $\boldsymbol{P}\neq\boldsymbol{I}$. To solve $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}$ for a general right-hand side $\boldsymbol{b}$, which triangular system is solved first?
options: $\boldsymbol{L}\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{b}$
$\boldsymbol{L}\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{b}$
$\boldsymbol{U}\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{b}$
$\boldsymbol{U}\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{b}$
